doc.title: Ray Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Chicago radio bands and remote broadcasts in the 1930s
summary: Sherman recalls listening to swing bands on Chicago radio from about 1935 and how remotes were miked and balanced.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Sure. I started thinking about that, I was really fortunate. I mean even, this was like in the late ‘30s, well I mean all through the ‘30s, but I mean starting to listen to the swing bands and whatever, from about ‘35 on, and just the local bands, on the local radio stations, everything was so great. Then eventually they had got the networks together. But I say just growing up when radio first started, and there was a lot of good bands in Chicago that you could listen to.
So many people mention the importance of radio in those days, and the live broadcasts too.
Oh no, that’s what I mean, yeah, all the remotes they called them.

It sounded good to me. I don’t know. Like we were talking about, you know when I did live T.V. and the balance was just terrible. And in those days they used to go — of course the bands just stayed in one place and the singer was there, they always knew it was the same set up. But they worked it out. And I don’t think they used more than two or three © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
mics maybe, one on the piano and one in the front of the band. It sounded great to me. I don’t know.
Well it was partly the musicians’ job to balance themselves, too, is that correct?

Well that’s what I say, I mean the guys went there and they were in a ballroom or whatever, a cafe, they played so it would sound good in the room. And it was up to the radio station to do what they could with that. But they didn’t seem to have any problem.
Well plus you weren’t comparing it to sound fidelity these days.
Oh no. I mean as far as the balance, you know, like all the instruments balanced correctly. I think they needed to put a mic in the piano probably.
